confidence_note: Book text not directly available; the violinist figures (8.6 hours a day, about an hour more than the average American, 2.8 hours of naps a week; sleep ranked second after practice) come from multiple chapter summaries and reader notes and match Ericsson's 1993 study. The Geoff case (CEO at 36, 4-6 hours of sleep, breakdown) rests on one detailed chapter summary: use only that a young CEO who slept little and travelled constantly broke down and could not work for weeks, without exact numbers. Old reference claims (4-5 hours of practice, 'those who slept the most' as the top trait, 'eight hours of sleep allow four hours of focus') are not supported and dropped. Editorial caveat: Ericsson's study was small and correlational.
facts: In Essentialism, McKeown opens the chapter on sleep with Geoff, a young CEO of a global microlending organization who travelled most of the year and slept only a few hours a night.
Geoff's health broke down; for weeks he could barely function.
McKeown then turns to K. Anders Ericsson's study of violinists, the research later popularized as the '10,000 hour' idea.
Ericsson's study compared violin students at a music academy in Berlin whom their teachers had sorted into the best and the merely good.
The best violinists practiced more than the merely good ones; McKeown points out that the second factor separating them was sleep.
The top players averaged 8.6 hours of sleep in every 24 hours, about an hour more than the average American, and napped about 2.8 hours a week.
The researchers' reading, which McKeown adopts: rest let the best players practice with greater concentration, so they got more out of each hour.

McKeown writes that sleep enhances your ability to explore, make connections and do less but better during your waking hours; the violin study is the one Malcolm Gladwell later popularized as the '10,000 hour rule'.
McKeown's argument: sleep protects the ability to choose well, which is the core skill of doing less but better.

Editorial caveat: Ericsson's group was small and the result shows the best slept more, not that sleep alone made them the best. The students recorded their own practice and sleep in diaries; no one was assigned an amount of sleep.
scene_details: a CEO living on a few hours of sleep between flights
tension: The famous study about practice hours contains a second, quieter finding most people skip.
opening_idea: Start with the number: 8.6 hours, in the study everyone cites for practice.

lessons.idea: Treat sleep as part of the work you want to do well, since tired people choose badly.
lessons.anchor: The best violinists practiced more and slept more; Geoff's breakdown.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A nurse finishing night shifts leaves the big decision about changing jobs until after two nights of proper sleep.

reflect_final: Which decision coming up this week would you rather make after a full night's sleep than at the end of a long day?

use_cases.situation: A colleague boasts about sleeping five hours to get more done.
use_cases.move: Mention that in Ericsson's violin study, cited by McKeown, the top players slept more than the good ones, not less.

use_cases.situation: Your team wants to make a big decision late in the evening.
use_cases.move: Propose deciding first thing tomorrow, after everyone has slept.

use_cases.situation: You are tempted to stay up to finish one more task.
use_cases.move: Write the next step on a note, close the laptop, and start with it in the morning.

pocket_idea: The best violinists practiced most and slept more; guard sleep as part of the work.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The study behind the 10,000-hour idea also found the best violinists slept about an hour more than the average American.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Ericsson's violinists: practice first, sleep second, 8.6 hours and naps; McKeown's point about choosing well; small-study caveat.
